newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain urges trucker unions to negotiate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain urges trucker unions to negotiate.

text.p: A truck drivers strike tightened its stranglehold on the Spanish economy as it entered its second week on Thursday and the government urged unions to come to the negotiating table.
The eight-day-old strike to demand better labour conditions has throttled roads in almost all of northern Spain, cut off supplies to many areas and forced factories to shut.
Unions warned the chaos was spreading south.
Representatives from the development, labour, economy and industry ministries met some transport associations on Thursday, but leading union Fedatrans, which called the strike, refused to join them.

"Those that are unwilling to join us at the negotiating table must change their stance because dialogue is the only way to find a solution to these problems," said Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado.
Strikers blocked a number of main roads and petrol stations and lined thousands of trucks along the hard shoulder of others, intimidating Spanish and foreign drivers who dared to pass.
A picket was run over and killed early on Thursday when he ran into the road to stop a French trucker from passing. The incident in the Burgos region was the most serious so far.
Truckers also blocked border crossings and six northern ports. Hundreds of foreign truckers found themselves caught in the jam.
In a mimic of the French truckers' strike last year which disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade, Spanish drivers are demanding a revamp of their sector.
In addition to reducing the retirement age to 60 years from 65, drivers are pushing for diesel subsidies, a revision of tariffs and recognition of professional illnesses.
Salgado said he would propose measures that would pave the way for lower diesel prices but that he needed more time to consider the other issues.
In the meantime, the Interior Ministry ordered security forces to guarantee essential supplies to towns. In some areas, the strike turned violent.

One driver was slightly injured on Wednesday when he was hit on the head by a stone while trying to fill up his truck at a petrol station in the Leon province. Pickets were also injured in clashes with police.
With the strike blocking supplies to many northern towns, companies were forced to halt production and send workers home.
Car manufacturers were worst hit. Renault's Spanish unit FASA-Renault said it would stop production on Thursday at plants in Valladolid and Palencia.
In the Basque region, France's Michelin was down to half capacity on Wednesday and said it would be paralysed from Thursday if the strike continued.

German producer Mercedez-Benz shut its plants in Barcelona and Vitoria, while production at General Motors unit Opel in Aragon, France's Citroen in Vigo and Nissan in Barcelona also ceased on Thursday.
Other companies including Firestone, Campofrio, and Asturiana del Zinc said they had also been disrupted by a lack of supplies.

Fedatrans warned the chaos would worsen and said it had brought another leading union on board, Fenadismer, while others were mulling a call to workers to take action. Taxi driver unions are also contemplating joining the strike from Monday.
Fedatrans said the only solution would be for the government to agree swiftly to their demands.
"To find a solution to this conflict, the cabinet must meet and approve the measures we are asking for," said Fedatrans spokesman Jon Mikel Abellanal.
The French government conceded to its drivers' demands during last year's strike including a clause on retirement at 55 instead of 60.
